300:
History On the morning of the 12th, in light rain, Zhang Chunqiao stood on a big truck fitted with loudspeakers and met the crowd at the coal yard. Someone shouted “take the umbrella away,” and he had the umbrella taken away. The complaints went on for five or six hours, and some women workers fainted. Zhang Chunqiao said the Shanghai Municipal Party Committee had carried out a wrong line, the crowd had been driven to act by the Municipal Party Committee, and he would not go back to Beijing until the problem was solved. About 500 people insisted on walking to Beijing. “Then Wang Hongwen agreed to go back, and without consulting us he took the 100-odd people from his mill back,” and people were “very dissatisfied” with this. Huang Jinhai proposed gathering at Culture Square, and Zhang Chunqiao agreed to send a dozen or so buses. See Huang Jinhai, Ten Years Not a Dream (《十年非梦》), ch. 4.

History In a phone report on the afternoon of the 12th, Zhen Wenjun said Zhang Chunqiao “at 7 this morning ... went to the site again to talk with the workers,” and “the workers object to Comrade Boda's letter, saying it only talks about production and says nothing about revolution.” See Wang Rui's paper.

Fiction The second option is a game branch.
301: Night of November 12 to evening of November 13, 1966
303: You took the No. 17 Mill people back to Yangshupu and spent the night at the mill. Only the next afternoon did you hear that Huang Jinhai had led the remaining 1,000-odd people into Culture Square, where they had waited all night. By the time you hurried over, the argument had already started in the dressing rooms backstage.
304: You came back to Culture Square on the last bus. It was past seven in the evening. Outside it was chaos. People were hungry and cold, and afraid the conservatives would storm in. Huang Jinhai called the demobilized soldiers up on stage. They cut white paper into squares and wrote “Picket” on the front, and he signed his own name on the back. Seven of the eight gates were shut. Only Gate 8, on Yongjia Road, stayed open. In the middle of the night he called the Communist Youth League members up on stage and sent them to the Municipal Party Committee reception office to ask for food.
305:
⟦0⟧

At half past two on the afternoon of the 13th, Zhang Chunqiao came in through Gate 8 in one car, with Xu Jingxian and a secretary. Red Guards from Beijing and Shanghai crowded backstage, pointed at him and called him a liar, with curses mixed in. He sat in a small room and did not answer back.

A little after three, Pan Guoping arrived with a group of Red Guards. The room was too small, so they moved to a large dressing room at the west end. Red Guards held the door and no one could get in. ⟦1⟧ The five points were worked out on the spot by Pan Guoping and a few Red Guards, everyone talking at once, arguing for an hour or two. Zhang Chunqiao added a sentence in parentheses after the second point, in his own hand.

⟦2⟧

Around five o'clock he signed. Huang Jinhai asked if he would go out front and say a few words to everyone, since they had waited a day and a night. He said yes.

Pan Guoping read out the five points. Zhang Chunqiao spoke, very slowly. He said the Municipal Party Committee had issued a notice yesterday, that when you went back you should not be attacked or blamed, and your wages would be paid as usual. But he could not promise you would not be besieged when you went back. He also said workers should carry on the tradition of hard work and plain living, and not be like some organizations that asked for cars, for tape recorders and cameras.

At first the people in the square did not take it in. Then someone shouted, and then thousands were shouting together. Huang Jinhai stood next to you, smoking. Ash fell on his padded jacket and he did not brush it off.

You knew what this piece of paper meant. Four days ago you were an illegal organization. Now the Municipal Party Committee was wrong and you were right. But you also saw Zhang Chunqiao, after he finished speaking, slowly fold up his script and look down at the crowd for a long time.
306: When you squeezed in, the five points were almost settled.
307: You were inside, standing against a dressing mirror.
308: Go up on stage and stand behind Zhang Chunqiao.
309: November 13　Culture Square rally. The Five Demands were signed, and the Workers' General Headquarters was recognized as a legal revolutionary organization.
310: November 13　Colluded with Zhang Chunqiao to sign the so-called “Five Demands,” paving the way for usurping Party and state power.
311: Stay below the stage, standing with the crowd.
312: November 13　Attended the Culture Square rally. The Workers' General Headquarters was recognized.
313: November 13　Attended the Culture Square rally.
314: Walk up to the microphone and read one article of the Constitution. Article 87. Citizens enjoy freedom of speech, of the press, of assembly, of association, of procession and of demonstration.
315: November 13　Read Article 87 of the Constitution at the Culture Square rally, setting out the workers' freedom of association.
316: November 13　Distorted the Constitution to champion an illegal organization.
317:
History Huang Jinhai brought more than 1,000 people back to Culture Square after 7 p.m. on the 12th, organized a paper-slip picket, and left only Gate 8 on Yongjia Road open. At 2:30 p.m. on the 13th, Zhang Chunqiao, Xu Jingxian and the secretary He Xiuwen came in and were abused by Red Guards. A little after 3, Pan Guoping arrived with Red Guards, and they negotiated in the large dressing room at the west end. The five points “were only worked out on the spot by Pan Guoping and a few Red Guards,” and the signing was at about 5. When Wang Hongwen went in, Huang Jinhai “did not notice.” Zhang Chunqiao's speech included lines such as “the Municipal Party Committee issued a notice yesterday, when you go back you should not be attacked or blamed, and wages will be paid as usual” and “do not be like some organizations that want cars, want tape recorders and cameras.” See Huang Jinhai, Ten Years Not a Dream (《十年非梦》), ch. 4.

Disputed The time of signing is 3:30 p.m. in “Anting Storm” and about 5 in Huang Jinhai. The sentence in parentheses in the second point, “in similar situations in future, a small number of representatives should be sent,” is said to have been added by Zhang Chunqiao in his own hand. See Wang Rui's paper. An hour before the signing, Zhang Chunqiao had just met the East China Bureau and the Municipal Party Committee on Kangping Road and agreed with the position Tao Zhu conveyed for the Center, which was to withhold recognition from the Workers' General Headquarters. See the 1979 materials of Mi Xinxiang, Cao Diqiu's secretary, quoted in Wang Rui.

History At a central meeting soon after, Mao Zedong took out the Constitution, read the passage on “freedom of association,” and asked, “Do workers have freedom of association or not? Do you read the Constitution or not?” He said, “On the Shanghai question, Zhang Chunqiao is right. First come the facts, then the policy.” See Wang Li, The First Year of the Cultural Revolution (《“文革”第一年》), quoted in Wang Rui. Wang Rui dates the meeting to November 16 from various accounts. Huang Jinhai records Mao saying at the Politburo meeting on November 15, “You can act first and report afterward. The facts always come before the concept.”

Fiction Wang Hongwen reading the Constitution at Culture Square is a game premise. It is the seed of the “freedom of association” dream.
321:
The 500 or so who would not come back walked north along the railway. They reached Kunshan and spent the night in the classrooms of Kunshan Middle School. You went there with the signed five points to persuade them to return to Shanghai.

Only when you arrived did you learn that the column had a new leader. The night before, a few people had held a meeting at Kunshan Middle School. They said a Party member should lead, and they chose a worker from the Shanghai Pulp Mill named Geng Jinzhang. He was in his early forties, spoke with a Shandong accent, and had been a soldier. He picked a few strong young men and formed a spearhead squad to handle security.

You stood at the front of the classroom and read the five points. When you got to the second one, someone below said the five points were fake. ⟦0⟧

The men of the spearhead squad closed in. You remembered someone grabbing your collar, desks knocked over, a fist hitting your cheekbone. Then a worker from No. 31 State Cotton Mill rushed in and pulled them off.

Half your face was swollen. Geng Jinzhang stood at the classroom door the whole time. He did not join in, and he did not stop it.
322: Someone else said, you pulled the No. 17 Mill people out at Anting, and now you come to fool us again.
323: Someone else said, the headquarters people left Anting first, and now they send you to fool us.
324: “If you won't listen, you bear all the consequences.” You left holding your face.
325: November 14　Went to Kunshan to mobilize the workers heading north to return to Shanghai.
327: You did not leave. You sat at the classroom door, waited until they were asleep, and copied the five points onto the blackboard one by one.
328: November 14　Went to Kunshan to mobilize the workers heading north to return to Shanghai, and publicized the Five Demands.
329:
History About 500 people walked north. At Kunshan Middle School, Geng Jinzhang, Zhou Baolin, Sun Yuxi and others staged a “coup.” “Because Geng was a Party member, the column was put under Geng Jinzhang of the Cement and Paper Mill,” and a “spearhead squad” was formed to handle security. Wang Hongwen hurried to Kunshan Middle School, told everyone that Zhang Chunqiao had signed the five points, and urged them to go back. “A few men of the ‘spearhead squad’ even beat Wang Hongwen up, his face was swollen.” Qiang Yulin of No. 31 Cotton Mill found out and stopped it. Wang Hongwen said, “If you won't listen, you bear all the consequences,” and went back. See Huang Jinhai, Ten Years Not a Dream (《十年非梦》), ch. 4 (Huang's account from Qiang Yulin).

Disputed Huang Jinhai gives Geng Jinzhang's factory as the “Cement and Paper Mill.” Other sources give the “Shanghai Pulp Mill” or the “Zhongni Paper Mill.”

Fiction The second option is a game branch. The details of the beating are dramatized for the game.
331: North Along the Railway · Kunshan · Suzhou
333:
Most people went back to Shanghai. The remaining 500 or so walked north along the railway, and you were among them.

⟦0⟧

By the second day many had blisters on their feet. Peasants along the way stood on the field ridges and watched. An old woman brought over a pot of hot water and did not ask a single question.

The night you stayed at Kunshan Middle School, a few people held a meeting and said a Party member should lead. You were a Party member too, but someone said you were a headquarters man, and the headquarters people had left Anting first. In the end they chose Geng Jinzhang of the Shanghai Pulp Mill. He was in his early forties, spoke with a Shandong accent, and had been a soldier. He picked a few strong young men and formed a spearhead squad. The next day ⟦1⟧ Wang Hongwen came to Kunshan Middle School to read the five points and was beaten up by the spearhead squad. You were in the corridor and heard desks crashing to the floor in the classroom.

In Suzhou, Huang Jinhai of No. 31 State Cotton Mill caught up too, saying he spoke for headquarters. Geng Jinzhang was afraid he would shake morale, so he shut him up in a bathhouse and had someone buy him flatbread to eat.

On the night of the 14th, Zhang Chunqiao caught up with them in Suzhou. Geng Jinzhang talked with him all night and put forward five demands again. On the 15th, at the Suzhou Railway Middle School, Zhang Chunqiao, Han Zheyi of the East China Bureau and Cao Diqiu of Shanghai all signed them. Zhang Chunqiao later told people that he and Cao Diqiu argued for two hours that day. Cao Diqiu would not sign, and he said, if you won't sign, I will.

Geng Jinzhang patted you on the shoulder and said, “Old Wang, this time we really walked our way out.”

On the 18th, the Municipal Party Committee sent a dozen or so coaches to bring you back to Shanghai. When you got off outside the Hongdu Theater, Geng Jinzhang told everyone not to scatter and to leave an address.
335: someone sent by the people around
336: Write your name and address in Geng Jinzhang's notebook too.
337: November 15　Met in Suzhou with Comrade Zhang Chunqiao, the Center's representative. The demands were met.
338: November 15　Led a mob roving to Suzhou to keep up pressure on the Center.
339: Go to the bathhouse and take Huang Jinhai a pot of hot water.
341: November 15　Led a mob roving to Suzhou.
342:
History About 500 people walked north. At Kunshan Middle School they made Geng Jinzhang their leader and formed a spearhead squad. Wang Hongwen went to Kunshan Middle School to urge them back and was beaten. Huang Jinhai caught up with them in Suzhou on November 14, and Geng Jinzhang held him in a bathhouse. On the evening of the 14th, Geng Jinzhang negotiated with Zhang Chunqiao and put forward Five Demands again, and Zhang Chunqiao, Han Zheyi and Cao Diqiu all signed. On the 15th a meeting was held at the Suzhou Railway Middle School. On the 18th the Municipal Party Committee sent vehicles to bring them back. When they got off outside the Hongdu Theater, Geng Jinzhang insisted on keeping a list of addresses. Afterward, on the basis of these 400 or so people, he built the “Second Regiment of Workers Returning to Shanghai from the North” of the Shanghai Workers' Revolutionary Rebel General Headquarters. See Huang Jinhai, Ten Years Not a Dream (《十年非梦》), ch. 4. Zhang Chunqiao's words “if you won't sign, I will” are from Ye Yonglie, The Rise and Fall of Wang Hongwen (《王洪文兴衰录》), p. 132, quoted in Wang Rui.

Disputed Wang Rui dates the Suzhou speech to November 16. Huang Jinhai records it as the evening of the 15th. A handover note once said Pan Guoping led people to Suzhou. Huang Jinhai says Pan Guoping went to Liuhe near Nanjing to bring back the people from the first train (later called the “First Regiment”).

Fiction Historically, Wang Hongwen took most people back to Shanghai and did not go to Suzhou. This section is a game branch. The old woman's hot water and Geng Jinzhang's words are dramatized for the game.
345: In late November 1966, the Shanghai College Red Guard Revolutionary Committee (the Red Revolutionaries) demanded that its paper, Red Guard Combat News, be inserted into Liberation Daily and distributed with it. The paper refused. Before dawn on November 30, the Red Revolutionaries stormed the paper's offices at 274 Hankou Road. The Workers' General Headquarters sent people to support them, and the Scarlet Guards surrounded them from outside. The standoff lasted eight days and nine nights, and the paper stopped publishing. On instructions from the Central Cultural Revolution Group an agreement was signed, and the paper came out again on December 7. Its significance is that this was the first time workers of Shanghai's two factions stood face to face in their tens of thousands, and each side remembered the other's faces. That a mass organization could force a Party paper to carry its sheet also showed that the Municipal Party Committee could no longer control its own mouthpiece.
347: The Shanghai College Red Guard Revolutionary Committee, made up mainly of students from Fudan, Jiaotong University and other schools. It was the most influential student rebel organization in Shanghai in the fall and winter of 1966. In the Liberation Daily Incident it stood with the Workers' General Headquarters. In late January 1967, angry that Zhang Chunqiao had taken the fruits of the January Revolution for himself, it launched “Bombard Zhang Chunqiao” and kidnapped Xu Jingxian. On January 30 the WGHQ took to the streets to suppress it, and it fell apart soon after. Its fate shows that the rebels were never one block. Students and workers, those who rose first and those who rose later, were soon fighting each other.
349: A tabloid run by the Red Revolutionaries. During the Cultural Revolution mass organizations ran hundreds upon hundreds of tabloids. They were one of the main sources of information at the time, and also the main weapon for attacking each other. Demanding that it be distributed with a Party paper amounted to demanding that the Party paper vouch for a mass organization.
353: On December 23, 1966, the Scarlet Guards held a rally in People's Square and put eight demands to Cao Diqiu. The first was recognition of the Scarlet Guards as a revolutionary mass organization. Cao Diqiu signed. The text of the other demands has yet to be found. On the 24th, Chen Pixian chaired a Secretariat meeting that judged the signature a mistake of political stance. On the 25th, at a rally of the Workers' General Headquarters and seven other organizations, Cao Diqiu announced that the signature was void. A little over a month earlier, the WGHQ had stopped a train for the same kind of signature. Now the Scarlet Guards had a signature, and two days later it was taken back. This document turned the two factions' positions upside down, and it led straight to Kangping Road.
356: The rebels' name for the conservatives, meaning people who protected the capitalist roaders as if they were “emperors.” After 1967, being called a royalist meant you had backed the wrong side. Members could not hold their heads up in their work units, and core members were put through struggle sessions and locked up. Most of those called this were Party members, model workers and workshop activists. They had thought they were the ones who listened to the Party most.
359: Kangping Road was where the Secretariat of the Shanghai Municipal Party Committee sat. On December 28, 1966, nearly 20,000 Scarlet Guards entered the compound to petition, demanding that the Municipal Party Committee account for voiding the signature. On the 29th, in Beijing, Zhang Chunqiao sent word through his wife Li Wenjing and through Xu Jingxian, telling the rebels “do not let the Scarlet Guards seize the fruits of victory.” Geng Jinzhang hurried back from Beijing and set up a command post. From 2 a.m. on the 30th, the Workers' General Headquarters and other organizations stormed the compound. By 6 a.m. more than 300 Scarlet Guards had been seized and 91 sent to hospital badly injured. At 7, 20,000 people filed out in single lines along six routes, and the armbands taken from them were piled in six big heaps. It is usually seen as the start of large-scale armed fighting in Shanghai. Zhang Chunqiao said afterward, “Once this battle was fought, the Municipal Party Committee was paralyzed. It collapsed.” For the Scarlet Guards, after this night their standing in their work units was never the same.
362: An order issued by the Workers' General Headquarters on December 31, 1966, demanding that “the bosses of the Shanghai headquarters of the Workers' Scarlet Guards and of all its district branches and sub-branches be arrested, every one, and handed over to the Public Security Bureau.” One mass organization issued arrest orders against another, and the Public Security Bureau took in whoever was on the list. In Shanghai in early 1967 this was normal. Later Wang Weiguo and others found that the public security system was holding large numbers of Scarlet Guards for no reason beyond “opposing Wang Hongwen” or “opposing the WGHQ.” The first round of checking recorded it as the “Urgent Order,” and the name here follows that record. The full text has yet to be found.
364: After Kangping Road, about 10,000 Scarlet Guards set off north on foot on the afternoon of December 30 to petition in Beijing. They reached Kunshan in Jiangsu on the afternoon of the 31st. The rebels chasing them arrived too, and in the clashes some trains on the Shanghai-Nanjing line were held up. On January 3, 1967, municipal Party secretary Ma Tianshui hurried to Kunshan to urge them back. In the end six or seven thousand still went to Beijing. Kunshan is the next station after Anting. Six weeks earlier the ones stopped were the rebels. This time they were the conservatives. The reasons for the two journeys north to petition were almost the same. The local authorities would not recognize them, so they went to the Center.
367: The process by which Shanghai's rebels seized power from the Municipal Party Committee and the city government in January 1967, officially called the “January Revolution” at the time. On January 4 and 5 they took over Wenhui Daily and Liberation Daily. On the 6th a rally overthrew the Municipal Party Committee, and after that the committee and the city government stopped functioning. On the 9th the Urgent Notice was published, and on the 11th four central bodies sent a joint telegram of congratulations. Mao Zedong said, “When the revolutionary forces in Shanghai rise up, there is hope for the whole country,” and power seizures soon swept the country. It was promoted as a model. Yet the Shanghai power seizure itself was carried out under the direct guidance of the Central Cultural Revolution Group. The so-called seizure of power by the masses from below had a hand from above from the very start.
369: Published in Wenhui Daily and Liberation Daily on January 9, 1967, signed by the Workers' General Headquarters and other rebel organizations (32 organizations by one account, 11 by another, to be checked), in ten articles. It called the early-January demands by workers for back pay, for making temporary workers permanent, and for people sent away to return to the city “economism.” It said these were a “new counterattack” launched on the economic front by the capitalist roaders in the Municipal Party Committee, and it called on people to “grasp revolution, promote production.” In its telegram of congratulations, the Center called it “entirely correct.” The irony is that the WGHQ had built itself on ordinary workers who had been persecuted and held down, and this notice told those same people to take their demands back.
371: Originally, a workers' movement that fought only for economic gains and ignored politics. In January 1967 Shanghai used it to label the wave of workers asking for money, for permanent status and to return to the city. Some work-unit leaders opened the floodgates and handed out money to protect themselves, and there were runs on the banks. That was real. Most of the demands were also real grievances piled up over years. Temporary workers had worked ten years and still could not be made permanent, and people sent away could not go home. That was real too. One label lumped the two together.
375: In the 1960s the state pushed “worker and peasant at once” rotation and the temporary and contract labor systems. These people did the same work without the wage grades, labor insurance and dossiers of permanent workers, and could be dismissed at a word. They were among the earliest and most determined rebels at the start of the Cultural Revolution, because they had almost nothing to lose. In early 1967 they asked to be made permanent, and the Urgent Notice branded this economism. The Center then issued a document banning nationwide temporary workers' organizations.
377: Proclaimed in People's Square on February 5, 1967. Its manifesto was titled “Long Live the Victory of the January Revolution.” Zhang Chunqiao was director, and Yao Wenyuan, Wang Hongwen and others were deputy directors. Preparations began on January 19, when Wang Hongwen was told to call the rebel leaders together and set up a new government on Paris Commune principles. It was first named the “New Shanghai Commune.” The manifesto itself said the leading members would be “elected by the revolutionary masses according to Paris Commune principles after the all-round seizure of power has succeeded,” and that “for the present” the rebel organizations would “consult and nominate” a provisional committee. That provisional committee was already a “three-in-one combination” of mass organizations, the heads of the army units in Shanghai, and revolutionary leading cadres. The manifesto also said “whoever cuts himself off from the masses ... must be replaced and purged at any time.” It never held a single election from beginning to end. Less than three weeks after it was founded, Mao Zedong asked, if every province is called a commune, what is the State Council called, what is the country called, and said, “better call it a revolutionary committee.” Its 19 days were the closest the Cultural Revolution came to the words “Paris Commune,” and they show most clearly that at the time the words were only a banner.
380: The practices of the Paris Commune of 1871, summed up by Marx in The Civil War in France. Public officials are chosen by universal suffrage and can be recalled at any time, and their pay is no higher than a skilled worker's. The Sixteen Points said the cultural revolution committees should “practice a system of general elections like that of the Paris Commune.” Li Xun's research points out that these principles were used during the Cultural Revolution to mobilize the masses against the old system and were dropped as soon as new governments were to be set up. Wang Hongwen later became Vice Chairman of the CCP Central Committee and still drew 64 yuan a month. This is perhaps the only trace these principles left.
383: The local organs of power set up after power seizures in the Cultural Revolution, made up of representatives of the army, “revolutionary leading cadres” and mass organizations in a “three-in-one combination.” On February 24, 1967, the Shanghai People's Commune was renamed the Shanghai Revolutionary Committee, and the provinces set up their own one after another. When Shanghai changed the name, not one person in the room was replaced, because the commune's provisional committee was already a three-in-one combination. What was really removed was the promise in the commune manifesto to hold elections on Paris Commune principles once the all-round seizure of power succeeded. Revolutionary committees were abolished step by step after 1978.
385: The rule for forming revolutionary committees, with representatives from the army, the cadres and the mass organizations. In Shanghai it was already written into the commune manifesto of February 5, 1967, which said the provisional committee would be a “three-in-one combination of revolutionary mass organizations, the heads of People's Liberation Army units stationed in Shanghai, and revolutionary leading cadres who uphold Chairman Mao's revolutionary line.” That was almost three weeks before the renaming. It was the way to restore order after the January power seizure. It brought the rebel leaders in and used the army and the veteran cadres to keep them in check. Ma Tianshui was the representative of the cadre side.
388: First secretary of the Shanghai Municipal Party Committee from November 1965. From April to December 1966 he was on sick leave with nasopharyngeal cancer, and Cao Diqiu ran the work. On December 24, while still ill, he chaired a Secretariat meeting that judged Cao Diqiu's signature recognizing the Scarlet Guards a mistake. On January 6, 1967, he was put through a struggle session in People's Square, and he was held and investigated for years afterward. After the Cultural Revolution he returned to work as first secretary of the Hubei Provincial Party Committee and a member of the Central Committee Secretariat. His memoir is At the Center of the January Storm (《在“一月风暴”的中心》). According to Wang Weiguo's posthumous manuscript, Wang Weiguo once released Chen Pixian from the custody of a special case group, which angered Zhang Chunqiao and Wang Hongwen.
391: Secretary of the Shanghai Municipal Party Secretariat, long in charge of industry. On January 6 he was struggled against with Chen Pixian and Cao Diqiu. Then, persuaded by Zhang Chunqiao, he “came over” and became the cadres' representative on the revolutionary committee. For the next ten years he ran Shanghai's industrial production. After October 1976 he took part in Shanghai's response, was placed under isolation and investigation, lost his mind, and died in a psychiatric hospital. He stood for another kind of person, a veteran cadre who knew production, kept his post by changing sides, and in the end was swallowed by that change.
394: Party branch secretary of the Shanghai Municipal Party Committee's writing group, known as “Xu the Third.” On December 18, 1966, he led the writing group in rebelling against the Municipal Party Committee, shouting “Burn Chen Pixian. Drag out Cao Diqiu. Down with Yang Xiguang. Smash Chang Xiping.” He was the mouthpiece of Zhang Chunqiao and Yao Wenyuan in Shanghai, and the phone message on the eve of Kangping Road went through him. On January 27, 1967, he was kidnapped by Fudan Red Guards, which set off “Bombard Zhang Chunqiao.” He later became a secretary of the Shanghai Municipal Party Committee. After 1976 he was sentenced to 18 years. In old age he wrote the memoir Ten Years, One Dream (《十年一梦》), which portrays Wang Hongwen negatively in many places. Huang Jinhai's memoir is called Ten Years Not a Dream (《十年非梦》), an answer to that book.
396: Geng Jinzhang's “Second Regiment of the Workers' General Headquarters.” In name it was under the WGHQ. In practice it was a system of its own. In early 1967 it claimed 500,000 to 600,000 members, and for a time it was bigger than WGHQ headquarters itself. Its core is said to be the people who refused to come back after Anting and followed Geng Jinzhang to Suzhou. In February 1967 Wang Hongwen set a trap and had Geng Jinzhang arrested, and the Second Regiment fell apart at once.
397: The large square in the center of Shanghai, once the racecourse. During the Cultural Revolution almost every citywide rally was held here, including the Scarlet Guards' rally on December 23, the rally that overthrew the Municipal Party Committee on January 6, and the founding rally of the Shanghai People's Commune on February 5.
399: Shanghai's other major daily. In November 1965 it published Yao Wenyuan's “On the New Historical Drama Hai Rui Dismissed from Office,” which started the Cultural Revolution. On January 4, 1967, the rebels took it over, the first step of the January Storm.
400: the one on the tracks at Anting
401: the one on the platform at Anting
402: Wang Hongwen of the Workers' General Headquarters
403: The Paris Commune Principles Took Hold
404: In Act Two, say no to the renaming. In Act Three, let the Shanghai Diesel workers vote for themselves.
405: Shanghai's commune committee members were elected by the factories and could be recalled, and this system lasted in Shanghai for ⟦0⟧. Over time the people elected gave way to people good at working connections, but the recall rule stayed. Everywhere else in the country, revolutionary committees were set up as before.
409: Say no to the renaming, then later call the army into the factory.
410: In 1967 Shanghai's commune committee members were elected once by the factories. After the army came into the factories, the lists were sent up by the Garrison Command, and in 1968 the name changed to revolutionary committee. Your dossier gained one more page. Defying the Chairman's instructions.
412: In Act One, read the Constitution. In Act Two, write freedom of association into Order No. 1. In Act Three, stamp the papers of the group that wants a “second great upheaval.”
413: In Shanghai, registering made a mass organization legal. Its aims were not reviewed, and those who used violence were dealt with under the criminal law. The armed fight at Shanghai Diesel never happened, and the people who beat Xie Fuxi to death were sentenced under the criminal law. The order was repealed a year later.
414: The Two Factions Sat at One Table
415: Go easy on the Scarlet Guards all the way.
416: Former Scarlet Guard workers joined the ⟦0⟧. People on both sides cursed you. Shanghai had no large opposing organization like the “Million Heroes” in Wuhan. That was the same as in history, only in this playthrough it came from sitting down and talking.
418: The Angang Constitution, Done for Real
419: When you return to No. 17 Mill in 1970, tear down that rule about fines.
420: No. 17 Mill's cadres worked in the workshops every week, and worker representatives elected by the workshops sat on the factory management meeting. Output fell for a month, then came back. ⟦0⟧
421: After the 1977 investigation, Article 14 went back up on the wall.
423: The night Nixon came to Shanghai in 1972, write a report.
424: Your report proposed opening Shanghai's port to American merchant ships first. It lay in a dossier for a year, then someone dug it out.
425: Workers Go Abroad to Learn Technology
426: In 1973, after $4.3 billion worth of equipment has been bought, decide who goes to learn.
427: The first 300 workers went to Japan, and later another group went to America. Jiang Qing called it slavish comprador philosophy. The machines at Jinshan ran smoothly half a year earlier than in history.
429: Refuse the gifts people bring, and keep refusing in Beijing.
430: As a Central Committee member and Vice Chairman, you still drew your wages from No. 17 Mill. You proposed that no cadre be paid more than a skilled worker in the same unit. No one approved it.
